nodes.text: On 14 October 1947 the Bell X-1, piloted by Chuck Yeager, became the first airplane to exceed the speed of sound at Mach 1.06.
nodes.sourceNote: Smithsonian NASM

nodes.text: The X-1 was air-launched from a B-29 and powered by a four-chamber Reaction Motors XLR11 rocket of 6,000 lbf burning liquid oxygen and ethyl alcohol.
nodes.sourceNote: Smithsonian NASM; chuckyeager.org; San Diego Air & Space Museum

nodes.text: The fuselage was modeled on the .50-caliber machine-gun bullet, a shape known to be stable at supersonic speed.
nodes.sourceNote: San Diego Air & Space Museum

nodes.text: The X-1 used extremely thin, strong wings (10 percent wing, 8 percent tail) to delay shock formation.
nodes.sourceNote: chuckyeager.org; National Interest

nodes.text: Bell was contracted on 16 March 1945 to build three XS-1 research aircraft, establishing the pure research aircraft concept.
nodes.sourceNote: San Diego Air & Space Museum

nodes.text: In early October 1947 Yeager lost elevator effectiveness at about Mach 0.92 due to shock-induced flow separation at the tail.
nodes.sourceNote: SPS Aviation

nodes.text: Dick Frost proposed the worm-gear arrangement letting the pilot drive the whole stabilizer; Yeager regained control with about two degrees of stabilizer on the following flight.
nodes.sourceNote: SPS Aviation

nodes.text: On the record flight the upgraded adjustable stabilizer let Yeager make fine angle changes that maintained pitch authority approaching Mach 1.
nodes.sourceNote: Smithsonian NASM

nodes.text: Tilting the entire stabilizer restores pitch authority because the full surface includes flow ahead of the shock, unlike the hinged elevator sitting in separated air.
nodes.sourceNote: National Interest; Smithsonian accounts; standard aerodynamics

nodes.text: The in-flight-adjustable stabilizer idea was proposed by NACA during the P-38 compressibility investigation and shelved; the concept became a defining control feature of the X-1.
nodes.sourceNote: Smithsonian Air & Space (EC VCL, P-38 package claim 8)

nodes.text: The movable-tail concept became standard on the supersonic fighters that followed, including the F-100, F-104, F-4, F-15, and F-16.
nodes.sourceNote: National Interest

nodes.text: Days before the flight Yeager broke two ribs falling from a horse, concealed it, and sealed the hatch using a broom handle cut by Jack Ridley.

nodes.text: Yeager, a WWII ace with 13 victories, named the aircraft Glamorous Glennis for his wife.

nodes.text: Augusta Ada Byron was born 10 December 1815, the same year as George Boole, daughter of the poet Lord Byron, and was raised on rigorous mathematics.
nodes.sourceNote: standard biography, multiple sources in pass

nodes.text: In 1833, aged 17, Lovelace met Charles Babbage and saw his Difference Engine demonstrated.
nodes.sourceNote: Two-Bit History

nodes.text: In 1840 Babbage gave his only public lecture on the Analytical Engine, in Turin; Luigi Menabrea published a French account in October 1842.
nodes.sourceNote: Note G Wikipedia; Things Have History

nodes.text: The Analytical Engine was a general machine design with a memory store, arithmetic mill, and punched-card instructions, and was never built.
nodes.sourceNote: Things Have History; standard references

nodes.text: Wheatstone suggested the translation, Babbage the notes; Lovelace worked about nine months in regular discussion with Babbage.
nodes.sourceNote: BBC Science Focus; Science Museum

nodes.text: The work was published in August 1843 in Taylor's Scientific Memoirs signed A.A.L.; of 66 pages, 41 are her notes.
nodes.sourceNote: BBC Science Focus

nodes.text: The notes' length relative to the original is reported as roughly three times by most sources and more than twice by Scientific American 1999.
nodes.sourceNote: Science Museum; Scientific American

nodes.text: It was the only extensive English paper on the Analytical Engine in Babbage's lifetime, and per Scientific American the only extended discussion of programming a computer for the next century.
nodes.sourceNote: Science Museum; Scientific American 1999

nodes.text: Note G is a step-by-step table for computing the recursively defined Bernoulli numbers, running 25 operations where Menabrea's longest example was 11, and containing a loop and superscript variable indexing.
nodes.sourceNote: Things Have History; Note G Wikipedia; Project Lovelace

nodes.text: Note G is called the first published algorithm, sometimes credited as the first computer program.
nodes.sourceNote: Science Museum

nodes.text: During the work Lovelace caught an error in Babbage's Bernoulli formulas, recorded in his 1864 memoir.
nodes.sourceNote: Note G Wikipedia

nodes.text: The published Note G table contains an error in operation 4, two variables swapped in a division, undetected for over a century until the program was run on modern computers; author or typesetter unknown.
nodes.sourceNote: Things Have History; pinned to the standard Note G reconstruction (2nd audit)

nodes.text: In Note A Lovelace wrote the Engine might act upon other things besides number if their relations could be expressed symbolically, giving musical composition as an example.
nodes.sourceNote: the Notes, via maketecheasier and Science Museum

nodes.text: Note G was collaborative, Babbage supplying the mathematics and earlier unpublished fragments, Lovelace authoring the published instruction sequence.
nodes.sourceNote: Note G Wikipedia; Misa scholarship via maketecheasier

nodes.text: Lovelace never saw her program run; the Analytical Engine has never been built, then or since. Babbage left only trial parts at his death in 1871, an 1878 committee advised against construction, and Plan 28's February 2025 report leaves the full physical engine still unbuilt. The Science Museum's Difference Engine No. 2 (1991-2002) is a different, simpler, non-programmable machine.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia, Analytical engine; Plan 28 project reports (verified by live search, this session)

nodes.text: Plan 28's research found it unclear whether Babbage's design could handle the indexed variables Lovelace's Bernoulli program required.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia, Analytical engine, citing Plan 28 as of May 2016 (BANKED, not used in the post; candidate beat for a future story)

nodes.text: Lovelace died in 1852 aged 36, two years before Boole's Laws of Thought was published.
nodes.sourceNote: Perplexity audit (standard dates, Wikipedia-cited)

nodes.text: The Lovelace objection, that the Engine has no pretensions to originate anything, later named by Turing in 1950, is attributed to Note G.
nodes.sourceNote: EC VCL (famous attribution; not anchored this pass)

nodes.text: George Boole met Charles Babbage at the 1862 Great London Exposition and wrote to him on 15 October 1862 promising to acquaint himself with Menabrea's paper, the one Lovelace had annotated; Boole died two years later.
nodes.sourceNote: Boole archive correspondence (Joseph Hill letter; Boole to Babbage, 15 Oct 1862), via agent audit

nodes.text: Notes A-F are signed A.A.L. but Note G itself was misprinted A.L.L., a typo in her initials on the note containing the first printed bug.
nodes.sourceNote: British Journal for the History of Mathematics (offprints study); HandWiki (BANKED; not used in the post)

nodes.text: Stein (1984) and the Lovelace-Babbage letters establish her authorship of the technical content more strongly than Babbage's 1864 memoir concedes.

nodes.text: George Boole was born 2 November 1815 in Lincoln, England, to a family of modest means and was self-taught beyond primary school.
nodes.sourceNote: Britannica; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

nodes.text: Boole taught school from age 16 to support his family and opened his own school at 20, studying mathematics from journals.
nodes.sourceNote: Britannica; Encyclopedia.com

nodes.text: Boole's system appeared in The Mathematical Analysis of Logic (1847) and in full in An Investigation of the Laws of Thought (1854) as a two-valued algebra of logic.
nodes.sourceNote: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Britannica

nodes.text: Boole wrote that logic should no longer be associated with metaphysics but with mathematics.
nodes.sourceNote: Encyclopedia.com (1847 work)

nodes.text: In 1844 the Royal Society awarded Boole its first gold medal for mathematics for On a General Method in Analysis.
nodes.sourceNote: History-Computer

nodes.text: In 1849 Boole, holding no university degree, was appointed first professor of mathematics at Queen's College Cork.
nodes.sourceNote: Britannica; History-Computer

nodes.text: Boole regarded the 1854 book as the mature statement of his ideas, titled as an investigation of the laws on which thought is founded.
nodes.sourceNote: Britannica

nodes.text: After 1854 Boole never published on logic again and was known in his lifetime chiefly for conventional mathematics.
nodes.sourceNote: Wolfram bicentenary essay; Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy

nodes.text: Boole received the Keith Medal in 1855, FRS in 1857, and honorary doctorates from Dublin and Oxford.
nodes.sourceNote: History-Computer

nodes.text: Boole married Mary Everest in 1855 and had five daughters.
nodes.sourceNote: Encyclopedia.com

nodes.text: In late 1864 Boole walked through a rainstorm, lectured in wet clothes, and died of pneumonia on 8 December 1864 at age 49.
nodes.sourceNote: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Encyclopedia.com; Wolfram

nodes.text: The cause of death is reported as pneumonia by most sources and as fever-induced pleural effusion by History-Computer.
nodes.sourceNote: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy; Britannica; History-Computer

nodes.text: The citizens of Lincoln installed a stained-glass window in Lincoln Cathedral in Boole's memory.
nodes.sourceNote: Encyclopedia.com

nodes.text: In 1937, 21-year-old Claude Shannon, tending the relay circuits of Vannevar Bush's Differential Analyzer at MIT, wrote a master's thesis showing that George Boole's two-valued algebra maps onto switching circuits.
nodes.sourceNote: EC Shannon package VCL (Smithsonian, Britannica, MIT accounts)

nodes.text: The correspondence runs both ways, circuits can be designed and simplified by algebra, and circuits can perform logic, so switches can compute.
nodes.sourceNote: EC Shannon package VCL

nodes.text: The thesis is routinely called the most important master's thesis ever written; Goldstine called it one of the most important.
nodes.sourceNote: EC Shannon package VCL (consensus phrasing; Goldstine quoted as "one of the most important")

nodes.text: Shannon knowingly used Boole's algebra, citing it in the thesis; there is no sign he knew of Lovelace's 1843 vision he was completing.
nodes.sourceNote: the thesis itself (Boole cited); Convergence Map audit round (the hedged second half)

nodes.text: Eleven years later at Bell Labs, Shannon published A Mathematical Theory of Communication (1948), founding information theory.
nodes.sourceNote: EC Shannon package VCL

nodes.text: Shannon lived to 2001, the only member of the Lovelace-Boole-Shannon arc who lived to see the digital age.
nodes.sourceNote: standard record; Convergence Map audit round

nodes.text: The Wrights designed their 1900 and 1901 gliders using the standard lift equation, Lilienthal's tables, and Smeaton's coefficient of 0.005, in use since the 1700s.
nodes.sourceNote: NASA Glenn Research Center; Smithsonian NASM

nodes.text: The 1901 glider developed roughly one third of predicted lift, with glides up to 300 feet.
nodes.sourceNote: NASA Glenn Research Center

nodes.text: The 1901 glider nose-dived repeatedly and once only the front elevator saved Wilbur's life.
nodes.sourceNote: National Park Service

nodes.text: The Wrights first tested the inherited data with a bicycle carrying a free-spinning horizontal wheel holding a model wing and a flat plate; the wing required an angle more than three times greater than Lilienthal's data predicted.
nodes.sourceNote: Smithsonian NASM; NASA Glenn Research Center

nodes.text: In fall 1901 they built a six-foot wooden wind tunnel in their bicycle shop, single-speed, fan-driven, read through a viewing window as balance dial angles.
nodes.sourceNote: NASA Glenn Research Center

nodes.text: The balances measured the ratio of a model wing's lift to a flat plate's drag in the same airflow, canceling air density, speed, and Smeaton's constant from the measurement.
nodes.sourceNote: NASA Glenn Research Center

nodes.text: They tested as many as 200 wing shapes made from 20-gauge steel strips, with detailed data recorded on dozens.
nodes.sourceNote: NASA Glenn Research Center; Smithsonian NASM

nodes.text: The number of shapes formally recorded is reported as about 30 by NASA and nearly 50 by the Smithsonian.
nodes.sourceNote: NASA Glenn Research Center; Smithsonian NASM

nodes.text: In the formal series they changed one design variable at a time, isolating the effect of camber, aspect ratio, and tip shape.
nodes.sourceNote: NASA Glenn Research Center

nodes.text: By mid-December 1901 the verdict was that Lilienthal's tables were largely correct and Smeaton's coefficient was wrong, with Lilienthal's camber inefficient.
nodes.sourceNote: National Park Service

nodes.text: The inherited 0.005 overstated the pressure by about fifty percent relative to the corrected value.
nodes.sourceNote: arithmetic on c-11; EC VCL

nodes.text: The 1902 glider, designed from the corrected data with longer, narrower wings and corrected camber, performed as calculated, with 700 or more glides that autumn, some over 600 feet.
nodes.sourceNote: MiGFlug; National Park Service; wright-house

nodes.text: The longest 1902 glide distance is reported variously as 622.5 and 662 feet.
nodes.sourceNote: wright-house; standard accounts

nodes.text: By December 1901 the Wrights had the aerodynamic data needed for a successful flying machine, and the 1903 propellers were designed as rotating wings from the same data.
nodes.sourceNote: Smithsonian NASM; standard accounts (propeller phrasing on audit watch)

nodes.text: Otto Lilienthal died in a glider crash in 1896.
nodes.sourceNote: standard record

nodes.sourceNote: EC VCL (research memory; open question)

nodes.text: The Tacoma Narrows Bridge opened on 1 July 1940 as the third-longest suspension span in the world.
nodes.sourceNote: WSDOT TNB history; Wikipedia (behind Golden Gate and George Washington)

nodes.text: Its designer Leon Moisseiff had worked on the Manhattan Bridge and the Golden Gate Bridge.
nodes.sourceNote: Moisseiff biographies (Wikipedia, PBS, Linda Hall); WSDOT

nodes.text: Moisseiff's deflection theory held that a long span could be far lighter and more flexible than tradition demanded.
nodes.sourceNote: WSDOT 1940-bridge and stories pages

nodes.text: The bridge used solid plate girders 8 feet deep in place of the 25-foot open stiffening trusses of the original state proposal.
nodes.sourceNote: WSDOT 1940-bridge page; Wikipedia

nodes.text: Construction workers nicknamed it Galloping Gertie because the deck rose and fell several feet in mild winds before the bridge opened.
nodes.sourceNote: WSDOT stories page; Wikipedia (roadway crews, May 1940)

nodes.text: Tie-down cables and hydraulic buffers were tried and did not stop the motion.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia; WSDOT (cables snapped; buffer seals damaged during sandblasting)

nodes.text: Professor F. Bert Farquharson of the University of Washington studied the bridge with wind-tunnel models and by 2 November 1940 had proposed a fix, deflectors to alter the airflow, unimplemented when the bridge fell five days later.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia; Live Science; WSDOT

nodes.text: The bridge collapsed on 7 November 1940 in a wind of about 40 mph, the deck twisting up to 45 degrees in a growing alternating motion, and fell into Puget Sound.
nodes.sourceNote: WSDOT collapse page; Wikipedia; APS News (some accounts say 42 mph; about 40 is safe)

nodes.text: The long-taught forced-resonance explanation is wrong; the wind was steady, with no rhythmic pulse matching a bridge frequency.
nodes.sourceNote: Billah and Scanlan 1991, Am. J. Phys. 59:118-124; WSDOT lessons page

nodes.text: In 1991 Billah and Scanlan published the correction identifying aeroelastic flutter, a self-excited negative-damping phenomenon, as the mechanism.
nodes.sourceNote: Billah and Scanlan 1991 (AIP, ADS)

nodes.text: In flutter the twisting deck reshapes the airflow so the aerodynamic force acts in the direction of the motion, adding energy each cycle.
nodes.sourceNote: Billah and Scanlan 1991; WSDOT bridges-failure page

nodes.text: One car remained on the deck; News Tribune editor Leonard Coatsworth crawled off largely on hands and knees, leaving his daughter's dog Tubby in the car.
nodes.sourceNote: WSDOT Tubby trivia page; HistoryLink; Wikipedia (about 500 yards to the tower)

nodes.text: Farquharson went onto the twisting span to try to rescue Tubby and was bitten for the attempt.
nodes.sourceNote: WSDOT Tubby trivia page; ASCE Civil Engineering Source (photographer Howard Clifford also attempted a rescue; the Farquharson account stands as written)

nodes.text: Tubby was the only life lost in the collapse.
nodes.sourceNote: WSDOT; Wikipedia; HistoryLink

nodes.text: The collapse effectively ended Moisseiff's career and the era of ever lighter, narrower, more flexible spans.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia (Moisseiff); SF Examiner; WSDOT (colleagues formally exonerated him; he died in 1943)

nodes.text: Since the collapse, wind-tunnel aerodynamic testing became standard practice for long-span suspension bridge design.
nodes.sourceNote: WSDOT bridges-failure page; Wikipedia

nodes.text: The tanker SS Schenectady, a welded wartime T2 sister type, split nearly in half at her dock on 16 January 1943 in calm weather shortly after sea trials, with a report heard about a mile away, the bow and stern sagging as the midsection rose.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia (SS Schenectady); bottom plates held, so nearly in half is the precise phrasing

nodes.text: Blame initially fell on the shipyards, fast work by inexperienced crews using still-new welding techniques.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia (SS Schenectady); Mariners' Museum

nodes.text: Constance Tipper, a metallurgist at Cambridge, showed the cracks did not initiate in the welds; the steel itself was the underlying problem.
nodes.sourceNote: Cambridge Engineering Department; Wikipedia (Constance Tipper); IMechE archive

nodes.text: The mechanism is the ductile-to-brittle transition; below a transition temperature the steel behaves in a brittle manner, and North Atlantic winter temperatures were low enough to cross that line.
nodes.sourceNote: Cambridge Engineering Department; Wikipedia (Constance Tipper)

nodes.text: Tipper was one of the first women to take the Natural Sciences Tripos at Cambridge. (AS PUBLISHED IN THE POST.)
nodes.sourceNote: Cambridge and Newnham history; the Tripos opened to women in 1881, over thirty years before Tipper sat it (1912-1915). The error circulates in secondary pages, including a Cambridge Engineering anniversary page. Correction recorded as c-liberty-ships-12. Editorial follow-up flagged to Fai.

nodes.text: In the 1940s the ductile-to-brittle transition was not widely understood by ship designers, which is why blame first fell on the welding.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia (Liberty ship); Mariners' Museum

nodes.text: A riveted hull tends to arrest a running crack at plate boundaries; a continuous welded hull lets a crack propagate, and the square corners of deck hatches acted as initiation points.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia (Liberty ship, SS Schenectady); later fixed with reinforcements and crack arrestors

nodes.text: Tipper's work contributed to a standard test for the temperature at which steel turns brittle, and steel selection for cold toughness in ships, bridges, and pipelines descends from this understanding.
nodes.sourceNote: Cambridge Engineering Department; Wikipedia (Constance Tipper); IMechE archive

nodes.text: Tipper's actual distinction at Cambridge: appointed Reader in 1949, she was the first and only full-time woman member of the Cambridge engineering faculty. (CORRECTION of c-08; not in the published post.)
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia (Constance Tipper); Cambridge Engineering Department

nodes.note: Retro-VCL backfill; see blocks/shannon_manchester-28m.md

nodes.label: Uncontained combustor failure and fuel fire during the aborted takeoff at Manchester, 22 August 1985; 55 die, 82 survive
AAIB Aircraft Accident Report 8/88 published with 31 safety recommendations

nodes.name: Arthur Bradbury
nodes.note: Purser who opened the left front door about 25 seconds after the aircraft stopped, then freed the jammed right front door. Name from secondary sources; the AAIB report does not name him.

nodes.text: On 22 August 1985, British Airtours Flight 28M, a Boeing 737-236, began its takeoff roll at Manchester bound for Corfu with 131 passengers and 6 crew.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 synopsis (0612 hrs, G-BGJL, 129 passengers plus 2 infants, runway 24)

nodes.text: At about 125 knots the pilots heard a thump, believed a tire had burst, aborted the takeoff cleanly, and turned off the runway.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 synopsis and 1.1 (thud at 125 kt; the commander thought tyre burst or bird strike; stop ordered in under a second)

nodes.text: A section of the left engine's combustion chamber, a part repaired by welding years earlier after a miscommunication over the repair manual, ruptured and was thrown out of the engine.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 findings 24-47 (No 9 combustor can, 160 mm crack fusion-welded November 1983, about 21 months earlier, so "years" in the post slightly overstates; subjective manual wording, a deleted crack-length limit, and finding 47's inadequate operator-manufacturer information exchange)

nodes.text: The ejected section struck a wing fuel tank access panel not built to take such an impact; fuel poured out and ignited.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 findings 53-55 (panel had roughly one quarter the impact strength of the wing skin; neither was required to meet impact criteria)

nodes.text: Stopped just off the runway, a light wind of about 7 knots pushed the burning fuel against the fuselage.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 synopsis, findings 6 and 62 (7 kt from 250 degrees; the wind called the principal factor controlling the fire)

nodes.text: The investigators found the crew had acted reasonably on everything they knew.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 section 2.3, finding 5 ("entirely reasonable based on the cues available to them")

nodes.text: The first fire vehicle reached the aircraft in under half a minute.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 sections 1.1 and 1.14, finding 79 (RIV2 at approximately 25 seconds after stopping)

nodes.text: Everyone survived the engine failure itself; the deaths came from the cabin, where burning interior materials produced dense toxic smoke, carbon monoxide and hydrogen cyanide, filling the cabin within minutes.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 cause statement, 1.13, findings 63-64 and 99 (48 of 54 on-board dead had CO and/or HCN above incapacitating levels; fire penetrated the cabin within about a minute of stopping)

nodes.text: The overwing hatch weighed 48 pounds and fell inward onto the passenger beside it.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 section 1.1 (fell pivoting about its lower edge across the passenger in seat 10F)

nodes.text: The gap to reach the overwing exit between the exit-row seats was 27 centimeters, ten and a half inches.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 section 1.15, finding 102 (10.5 inches measured between row 10 cushions and row 9 seat backs)

nodes.text: Most of those who died were found in the part of the cabin around the overwing exit.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 section 2.7.2 (approximately 38 of 54 recovered from rows 8-12, the overwing exit zone)

nodes.text: The purser fought a jammed door, abandoned it, and had the opposite door and slide working about 25 seconds after the aircraft stopped. (AS PUBLISHED IN THE POST; the door sides are reversed.)
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 sections 1.1 and 2.7, finding 100. The RIGHT front door (R1) jammed from a slide container lid design fault; the purser opened the LEFT front door (L1) about 25 seconds after stopping and freed R1 about 1 minute 10 seconds after stopping. Correction recorded as c-manchester-28m-16. Editorial follow-up flagged to Fai.

nodes.text: That working front door is a large part of why 82 people lived.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 sections 1.2 and 1.15, findings 97-98 (82 survived, 55 died: 53 passengers and 2 rear cabin crew; one survivor died 6 days later in hospital)

nodes.text: The investigation produced 31 recommendations.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 section 4, recommendations 4.1 through 4.31; SKYbrary

nodes.text: The required clear space at overwing exits, and crew checking that the people sitting there can open them, trace to this accident.
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 recommendations 4.10-4.11; CAA access-space rules; SKYbrary and Wikipedia on exit-row briefing requirements (the "willing and able" wording is the later regulatory formulation)

nodes.text: The jammed forward door was the right (R1), from a slide container lid design fault; the purser opened the left front door (L1) about 25 seconds after the aircraft stopped and freed R1 about 1 minute 10 seconds after stopping. (CORRECTION of c-12; not in the published post.)
nodes.sourceNote: AAIB 8/88 sections 1.1 and 2.7, finding 100

nodes.name: Lockheed Constellation
nodes.note: Added from block 2026-07-22; see blocks/shannon_constellation.md

nodes.label: TWA, driven by major stockholder Howard Hughes, asks Lockheed for a 40-passenger transcontinental airliner with about 3,500 mile range
Constellation first flight
Hughes and TWA president Jack Frye fly Burbank to Washington in 6 hours 57 minutes; on the return trip they later give Orville Wright his last flight at Wright Field

nodes.name: Howard Hughes
nodes.note: TWA major stockholder; set the requirement that forced the design and later flew the record transcontinental leg.

nodes.name: Jack Frye
nodes.note: TWA president; co-pilot on the April 1944 record flight.

nodes.text: Lockheed had worked since 1937 on the L-044 Excalibur; in 1939 TWA, at Howard Hughes's instigation, requested a 40-passenger transcontinental airliner with about 3,500 miles range, beyond the Excalibur's capability, producing the L-049 Constellation.
nodes.sourceNote: USNI Naval History; Military Wiki; Grokipedia

nodes.text: The Lockheed team included president Robert Gross, chief engineer Hall Hibbard, and chief research engineer Kelly Johnson.
nodes.sourceNote: united-states-lines; Grokipedia; Military Wiki

nodes.text: A single vertical fin tall enough for the required directional stability would not have fit inside TWA's existing hangars, so Lockheed split the fin area into three shorter fins to keep overall height down.
nodes.sourceNote: USNI Naval History; MiGFlug

nodes.text: The triple tail also sat high enough to clear the prop wash and added stability.
nodes.sourceNote: united-states-lines

nodes.text: Directional stability scales with fin area and moment arm rather than the height of any single fin, so three shorter fins of equivalent total area preserve authority while reducing height, at the cost of additional parts, joints, junction drag, and tail structure.
nodes.sourceNote: standard aerodynamics; house explanation derived from c-constellation-03 and -04

nodes.text: The aircraft stood unusually tall for its era because its very long propellers required ground clearance.
nodes.sourceNote: united-states-lines

nodes.text: The fuselage sloped downward from the tail in the graceful dolphin curvature.
nodes.sourceNote: united-states-lines; USNI; Military Wiki. The popular stretched-airfoil explanation is unverified and not used.

nodes.text: The Constellation had a fully pressurized cabin, among the first on an airliner, allowing cruise above 20,000 feet, over the weather that afflicted the DC-3 and DC-4, at more than 300 mph.
nodes.sourceNote: MiGFlug; Grokipedia

nodes.text: First flight January 9, 1943.
nodes.sourceNote: Grokipedia; MiGFlug

nodes.text: On April 17, 1944, the second production C-69, piloted by Howard Hughes and Jack Frye, flew Burbank to Washington in 6 hours 57 minutes, about 2,300 miles at roughly 330 mph.
nodes.sourceNote: Military Wiki

nodes.text: On the return trip the aircraft stopped at Wright Field and gave Orville Wright his last flight, more than 40 years after his first; he remarked that the Constellation's wingspan was longer than the distance of his first flight. The Wright Field stop is dated April 26, 1944; the April 17 record leg was outbound.
nodes.sourceNote: Military Wiki

nodes.text: The L-049 Constellation's wingspan of 123 feet exceeds the 120 feet covered by the first powered flight. The 123 ft 5 in figure is the later C-121 stretch.
nodes.sourceNote: Grokipedia specs; Wright first-flight record (EC Wright wind tunnel VCL)

nodes.text: 856 Constellations were built across numerous models, most powered by four 18-cylinder Wright R-3350 radials; the type served as Eisenhower's presidential aircraft and in the Berlin Airlift.
nodes.sourceNote: Military Wiki

nodes.text: Willis Hawkins maintained the Excalibur program was purely a cover for the Constellation.
nodes.sourceNote: Military Wiki (Hawkins); USNI hedges it as 'some aviation authorities contend'; the L-044 was a legitimate funded study predating Hughes, so the pure-cover framing is disputed. Texture only, not used in copy.

A-12 first flight at Groom Lake
Declared fully operational at design specifications, sustained Mach 3.2 at 90,000 feet

nodes.name: Richard Bissell
nodes.note: CIA Deputy Director for Plans; convened the RCS work that became RAINBOW and drove the U-2 successor program.

nodes.name: Edwin Land
nodes.note: Chaired the review panel that twice declined to select Lockheed's design before the A-12 won.

nodes.name: Francis Gary Powers
nodes.note: His U-2 was shot down over the Soviet Union in May 1960, during A-12 development, confirming the threat the program answered.

nodes.text: After Soviet protests over U-2 overflights, Bissell convened the first meeting on reducing the U-2's radar cross section on Aug 16, 1956; the resulting Project RAINBOW failed to reduce RCS enough.
nodes.sourceNote: Skytamer timeline; Wikipedia; CIA/Robarge

nodes.text: On April 21, 1958 Johnson made his first notes on a Mach 3 aircraft, initially called U-3, which evolved into Archangel I.
nodes.sourceNote: Skytamer

nodes.text: Johnson and Bissell agreed there should be one more round before satellites made aircraft reconnaissance obsolete for covert work.
nodes.sourceNote: Johnson quoted in Wikipedia; CIA/Robarge

nodes.text: The U-2 program was code-named ANGEL, so the successor designs were nicknamed ARCHANGEL, running A-1 through A-11; the A-12 was the twelfth internal design effort.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia; The Aviationist; National Interest

nodes.text: In Nov 1958 the Land Panel provisionally selected Convair's FISH over Lockheed's A-3; in June 1959 it provisionally selected Lockheed's A-11 over FISH and instructed both companies to redesign.
nodes.sourceNote: Skytamer

nodes.text: On Sept 14, 1959 the CIA selected the A-12 over Convair's KINGFISH and established Project OXCART.
nodes.sourceNote: Skytamer; Wikipedia

nodes.text: CIA representatives initially favoured Convair's design for its smaller radar cross section; the A-12 won on slightly better specifications, much lower projected cost, and track record, Convair's B-58 having run late and over budget while Lockheed delivered the U-2 on time and under budget.
nodes.sourceNote: Wikipedia (explicit)

nodes.text: Sustained Mach 3.2 heats the airframe past 250 degrees C, beyond aluminium's tolerance, so the aircraft was built overwhelmingly from titanium alloy.
nodes.sourceNote: MiGFlug; CIA/Robarge

nodes.text: Titanium forced new manufacturing: Skunk Works had to invent new tools, welding methods, and inspection procedures. Titanium conducts heat poorly, so cutting heat concentrates at the tool edge and destroys conventional tooling, and hot titanium absorbs oxygen and nitrogen from air and embrittles, requiring inert-gas shielded welding.
nodes.sourceNote: MiGFlug; CIA.gov OXCART (innovations in titanium fabrication); mechanism is standard materials engineering

nodes.text: Much of the titanium was reportedly acquired covertly through shell companies from Soviet-controlled sources, the only place to obtain it in quantity.
nodes.sourceNote: Declassified CIA documents and Ben Rich's memoir; dummy corporations purchased rutile ore through third countries sourcing from the USSR. Attribution and the 'much of' hedge are carried in the copy.

nodes.text: Testing was conducted from Groom Lake, a dry lakebed in Nevada.
nodes.sourceNote: 19FortyFive; standard record

nodes.text: In 1965 the A-12 was declared fully operational at its design specifications, sustained Mach 3.2 at 90,000 feet, after hundreds of hours flown at high personal risk by CIA and Lockheed pilots.
nodes.sourceNote: CIA.gov OXCART page (official)

nodes.text: Fifteen A-12s were built (12 single-seat recon, 1 two-seat trainer, 2 M-21 drone carriers; the 32 SR-71s and 3 YF-12s are separate programs); the type retired in 1968, and the two-seat Air Force derivative, the SR-71, became far better known.
nodes.sourceNote: The Aviationist; MiGFlug; standard record

nodes.text: Titanium's reactivity caused documented shop failures: cadmium traces from plated wrenches produced galvanic corrosion and bolt failure at temperature, and spot welds failed seasonally because Burbank raised chlorine levels in summer municipal water against algae, attacking the titanium during washing.
nodes.sourceNote: Ben Rich. Banked, held out of the post for length, cleared for comment-thread use.

nodes.label: Ronan Point, a 22-storey Large Panel System tower, opens in Canning Town, Newham, East London
A gas explosion in an 18th-floor corner flat blows out a load-bearing flank wall; the south-east corner progressively collapses top to bottom
The 5th Amendment to the UK Building Regulations introduces disproportionate collapse: a building must not collapse to an extent disproportionate to its cause

nodes.name: Ivy Hodge
nodes.note: Resident of flat 90 on the 18th floor; lit a match for her gas stove at about 5:45am on 16 May 1968 and survived the explosion that triggered the collapse. That she survived is the point: the blast was small; the building's response was the disaster.

nodes.text: Ronan Point was a 22-storey tower in Canning Town, Newham, East London, opened March 1968.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: It was built using a Large Panel System (Taylor Woodrow Anglian / Larsen-Nielsen), precast concrete panels bolted together with no structural frame.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: At about 5:45am on 16 May 1968, resident Ivy Hodge lit a match for her gas stove in flat 90, an 18th-floor corner flat.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: A gas explosion, from a faulty connection on the cooker supply, blew out a load-bearing flank wall panel supporting the flats above.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: With the wall gone, the floors above lost support and fell, each pancaking onto the next, a progressive collapse of the building's south-east corner, top to bottom.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: Four of the 260 residents died and 17 were injured; the toll was low because the building had just opened and most flats above were unoccupied.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: The Tribunal found the progressive collapse was inherent in the design, not just bad workmanship; the building lacked alternate load paths.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: The Larsen-Nielsen system was designed for buildings up to about 6 storeys; it was extended to 22.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: Investigation found appalling workmanship at joints (some load-bearing joints with less than 50 percent mortar; some later found packed with newspaper and tin cans).
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: The disaster led to the 5th Amendment to the UK Building Regulations (1970), introducing disproportionate collapse: a building must not collapse to an extent disproportionate to the cause.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: As an interim measure, buildings over five storeys built after November 1968 had to resist an explosive pressure of about 34 kPa (about 5 psi).
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: The concept spread internationally; US and other codes adopted structural integrity and robustness provisions traceable to Ronan Point.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: The fix in principle is to tie elements together at joints and provide alternate load paths so loads redistribute if one element fails.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.text: The disaster effectively ended Large Panel System construction in the UK.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 numbered VCL, verbatim per Rule 1

nodes.name: Bela Barenyi
nodes.note: Daimler-Benz engineer (1907-1997; at the company 1939-1974). Challenged the belief that a safe car must be rigid, and patented the opposite: a rigid passenger cell with crumple zones that absorb energy by deforming. Held a very large number of patents (Mercedes cites more than 2,500).

nodes.text: The physics is impulse-momentum: force times time equals change in momentum; momentum change is fixed by mass and speed, so extending the collision time lowers the average and peak force on occupants.

nodes.text: A rigid car stops almost instantly, producing a huge force spike transferred to occupants; a crumpling car extends the stop by a few tenths of a second, dramatically lowering peak force.

nodes.name: NASA 3D-printed combustion chamber (GRCop-42, Marshall 2021)
nodes.note: Retro-VCL backfill; see blocks/shannon_nasa-printed-chamber.md

nodes.title: EC V5 fact-check: NASA GRCop-42 printed chamber (2021 Marshall hot-fire; NASA paper and trade coverage)

nodes.label: A 3D-printed GRCop-42 combustion chamber is hot-fire tested at Marshall (Test Stand 115); about 9 seconds in, the nozzle extension fails first, then the chamber wall tears and the barrel separates
Sectioning reveals the chamber split along a build-interruption witness line, at porosity three orders of magnitude above a clean print; NASA's lesson is process rigor, not abandoning the method

nodes.text: In February 2021, at NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center, a combustion chamber, 3D-printed from GRCop-42, a copper alloy NASA developed to survive a rocket engine's heat, went on the test stand.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 fact-check (NASA paper; date and place Feb 9 2021, Marshall Test Stand 115; GRCop-42 copper-chromium-niobium alloy, both confirmed)

nodes.text: About nine seconds into the burn the first crack appeared in the experimental nozzle, which fragmented and broke away; a couple of seconds later hot gas tore through the chamber wall and the barrel fully separated.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 fact-check (NASA paper; about 9 s, carbon-carbon nozzle extension fails first, then the chamber, sequence confirmed)

nodes.text: During the print months earlier the build had stopped and restarted four times (a power loss, a brownout, and two points where overflow powder was cleared by hand); each interruption can leave a faint horizontal witness line where it resumed.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 fact-check (NASA paper; build-interruption witness line confirmed)

nodes.text: The chamber had split exactly along one of those witness lines.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 fact-check (NASA paper; failure originated at a build-interruption witness line)

nodes.text: The interruptions themselves did not doom the part: NASA printed test bars with the same deliberate pauses and those came out perfectly strong, so a clean restart does not weaken the metal.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 fact-check (NASA paper; replica-interruption test bars showed no degradation, confirmed as the paper's finding)

nodes.text: Sectioning found porosity, microscopic voids, at levels three orders of magnitude (a thousand times) higher than a clean print should have, lack-of-fusion defects pointing to a subtle process problem during the interrupted layer that build logs and nominal laser readings never revealed.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 fact-check (NASA paper; three orders of magnitude higher than typical GRCop-42 directly confirmed, multiple sources)

nodes.text: The pre-test CT scans were focused on verifying powder removal, not on hunting for witness lines, so a part with a built-in weak spot passed every check and only revealed the defect when cut open after failure.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 fact-check (NASA paper; inspection focus consistent with the build-records-looked-fine narrative)

nodes.text: NASA's lesson was not "stop interrupting builds" or "don't trust the alloy" but process rigor: print witness coupons alongside the real part that can be cut open and tested, inspect for the specific failure mode, and never assume a clean-looking build is a sound one.
nodes.sourceNote: EC V5 fact-check (consistent with the paper's conclusions)

nodes.title: EC retro-VCL: ASML and EUV lithography (published caption; ASML, ZEISS SMT, TRUMPF/world-of-photonics, Silicon Canals, TrendForce)

nodes.label: By the 2000s, with 193 nm DUV light stretched by immersion and multi-patterning, the most advanced chip layers need a shorter wavelength; ASML industrializes extreme ultraviolet lithography

nodes.text: Lithography prints patterns onto silicon; for years the industry stretched 193 nm deep-ultraviolet light with immersion, multi-patterning, and process tricks, but the most advanced chip layers needed a different answer.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; ASML (DUV immersion and multi-patterning history)

nodes.text: ASML helped industrialize extreme ultraviolet lithography using 13.5 nm light, more than 14 times shorter than the 193 nm deep-UV light used before.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; ASML (13.5 nanometers, more than 14 times shorter than DUV light)

nodes.text: EUV light is absorbed by almost everything, air and glass included, and normal lenses do not work, so ASML's machines guide the light through high vacuum using mirrors instead of lenses.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; ZEISS (EUV absorbed by all materials including air; reflective optics in a vacuum chamber)

nodes.text: There is no simple EUV bulb; ASML generates the light by firing laser pulses at fast-moving droplets of molten tin, a first pulse reshaping the droplet and a second vaporizing it into plasma.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; ASML (laser-produced-plasma source; pre-pulse flattens, main pulse vaporizes); ZEISS; TRUMPF

nodes.text: That tin-droplet process happens up to 50,000 times per second.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; ASML and ZEISS (50,000 times every second; 50,000 droplets of tin every second)

nodes.text: The plasma reaches about 220,000 degrees C, almost 40 times hotter than the surface of the Sun.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; ZEISS and world-of-photonics (nearly 220,000 degrees Celsius, almost 40 times hotter than the sun)

nodes.text: The EUV light from the plasma is collected by mirrors, guided through the machine, and used to expose patterns into photoresist on a wafer, repeatedly, inside factories that need precision, uptime, cleanliness, and repeatability.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; ASML; Silicon Canals (collector mirror, optical column, mask, wafer)

nodes.text: ASML did not just build a machine that makes light; it industrialized a form of light difficult to create, collect, transport, and use.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption (characterisation supported by the technical claims above)

nodes.text: Because advanced chipmakers needed EUV so badly, Intel, TSMC, and Samsung helped fund ASML's next-generation lithography development.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; TrendForce (Intel, TSMC, Samsung as main clients and co-investors in ASML's development)

nodes.note: Sega CEO who agreed to invest $5 million in NVIDIA after the NV2 contract collapsed, providing the runway that saved the company.

nodes.text: In 1996 NVIDIA had one month of payroll left: its first chip had failed and Microsoft had made its architecture obsolete in a single product announcement.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; Wikipedia RIVA 128; Tom's Hardware (1996 near-bankruptcy, DirectX obsoleting NV1)

nodes.text: NVIDIA was three years old and had bet the company on the NV1, which used quadrilaterals for 3D instead of triangles, matching Sega's Saturn to try to win the console-to-PC port market; Sega even signed an exclusive contract for the next-generation chip.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; Wikipedia; vintage3d; Grokipedia (NV1 quadratic/quadrilateral rendering; Sega partnership)

nodes.text: Then Microsoft launched DirectX, which standardized on triangle primitives only; the PC industry followed, the NV1 flopped, and the Sega NV2 follow-up contract was effectively dead.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; Wikipedia; Grokipedia (Direct3D triangle standard; NV1 failure; NV2 cancellation)

nodes.text: Jensen Huang cut headcount from around 100 to 40.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; Wikipedia (laid off half of about 100); Medium/TheBigCollapse (shrinking to just 30)

nodes.text: Huang flew to Sega's headquarters, told CEO Shoichiro Irimajiri that NVIDIA couldn't deliver the NV2, and asked him to invest $5 million anyway; Sega said yes.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; Yahoo Finance; Tom's Hardware; BGR (Huang proposed converting owed contract money into a $5M equity investment; Irimajiri agreed)

nodes.text: That cash bought NVIDIA months, not years, of runway; a normal chip cycle took well over a year of tape-outs and re-spins, which NVIDIA could not afford even once.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; BGR (six months to live); industry norms

nodes.text: Huang spent roughly a third of the remaining money on emulation software; the emulator was so slow that a single frame took about 30 seconds, but it let NVIDIA design and verify a new chip entirely in software and send it straight to SGS-Thomson for first silicon, with the company finished if that silicon failed.
nodes.sourceNote: Published caption; Medium/Hermansson ($1M in the bank, half spent on the emulator); 86Box (SGS-Thomson milestone payments; driver emulation architecture)

nodes.text: The chip was RIVA 128; it shipped in August 1997 when NVIDIA again had about one month of payroll left, supported only 8 of the 24 alpha blend modes it was supposed to, but performance crushed competitors, and NVIDIA sold over one million units in four months.

nodes.text: NVIDIA survived, went public in 1999, and the simulation-first approach that began as a desperation hack became a permanent advantage that helps it ship better silicon on first tape-out than most rivals; the company is worth around $5 trillion today.

nodes.title: EC VCL: point-contact transistor (dual Perplexity and Gemini audit; IEEE Spectrum, Computer History Museum, Wikipedia, ETHW, The Register, ScienceDirect, CHM Revolution, allaboutcircuits)

nodes.label: William Shockley conceives a field-effect amplifier at Bell Labs; it fails to work as intended
Bardeen and Brattain's point-contact device amplifies a signal through germanium, the first working transistor
The device is demonstrated to Bell Labs officials, amplifying a voice with no vacuum tube in the circuit; Shockley calls it a magnificent Christmas present
Within months Shockley conceives the junction transistor, the sturdier manufacturable design; John Pierce names the device transistor by colleague vote
Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley share the Nobel Prize in Physics

nodes.name: John Bardeen
nodes.note: Bell Labs theorist. Diagnosed why Shockley's field-effect amplifier failed (surface states blocking the field), then with Brattain built the point-contact device around the obstacle. Shared the 1956 Nobel; later won a second Nobel in Physics in 1972 for superconductivity, the only person to win two in the field.

nodes.name: Walter Brattain
nodes.note: Bell Labs experimental physicist. Solved the contact-spacing problem with a razor: one strip of gold foil over a plastic triangle, sliced at the tip to make two contacts a blade's width apart. Shared the 1956 Nobel.

nodes.name: William Shockley
nodes.note: Organized the solid-state group; his 1945 field-effect idea failed, but the junction transistor he then conceived became the manufacturable design. Shared the 1956 Nobel. Later founded Shockley Semiconductor, whose defectors (the Traitorous Eight, including Robert Noyce, the line's namesake) founded Fairchild.

nodes.name: John Pierce
nodes.note: Bell Labs engineer who coined the name transistor (transconductance or transfer, plus varistor), chosen by colleague vote in 1948.

nodes.text: Before transistors, electronics relied on vacuum tubes: electrodes in an evacuated bulb functioning as amplifiers and switches, hot, fragile, power-hungry, with a warm-up delay.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [1][3] (IEEE Spectrum; ETHW demonstration account)

nodes.text: Bell Labs pursued a solid-state replacement for the unreliable vacuum tubes and electromechanical switches in the Bell Telephone System.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [2] (Computer History Museum)

nodes.text: In April 1945 Shockley conceived a field-effect amplifier; it failed to work as intended.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [5] (Computer History Museum; Gemini-confirmed)

nodes.text: John Bardeen worked out why: electrons gathering at the semiconductor's surface (surface states) were blocking the electric field from penetrating the material.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [6] (Computer History Museum)

nodes.text: Bardeen and Brattain then pursued a point-contact approach through the surface rather than the field effect.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [7] (IEEE Spectrum)

nodes.text: The design required two gold contacts touching the germanium closer together than anyone could mount two separate wires; Brattain attached one strip of gold foil over the point of a plastic triangle and sliced through the gold at the tip, producing two isolated contacts a blade's width apart (under about 0.1 mm at the surface).
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [8][9] (Wikipedia; allaboutcircuits; Gemini gave about 0.002 in)

nodes.text: On December 16, 1947, the critical experiment worked: a block of germanium with two closely spaced gold contacts held by a spring; the voltage on one contact modulated the current through the other, amplifying the input up to 100 times.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [8][10] (Wikipedia; Computer History Museum)

nodes.text: Mechanism: the germanium surface had an excess of electrons; the incoming signal injected holes (an absence of electrons that carries current), creating a thin layer with a scarcity of electrons and letting a small change at one contact steer a larger current at the other.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [11] (Wikipedia; experimentally discovered, not predicted)

nodes.text: On December 23, 1947, the device was demonstrated to lab officials, switched in and out of an audio circuit so they could hear the amplification, instant, with no warm-up; Shockley called it a magnificent Christmas present.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [12][13] (ETHW; Computer History Museum, quote as attributed)

nodes.text: In 1948 Shockley conceived the more robust junction transistor (built 1951), the first practical and manufacturable transistor design.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [16] (CHM Revolution; ScienceDirect; US Patent 2,569,347)

nodes.text: The device was named transistor by engineer John Pierce, a combination of transconductance or transfer and varistor, chosen by colleague vote in 1948.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [14] (The Register, quoting the Bell Labs voting paper)

nodes.text: Bardeen, Brattain, and Shockley shared the 1956 Nobel Prize in Physics.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [17] (CHM Revolution)

nodes.text: ENIAC, completed in 1946, ran on about 18,000 vacuum tubes and filled a room; modern chips hold billions of transistors.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL (ENIAC about 17,468 tubes, about 18,000 defensible; present-day comparison)

nodes.name: The vacuum tube's limits (heat, fragility, power draw, no miniaturization) as the barrier to modern electronics
The junction transistor and every solid-state device downstream of it

nodes.title: EC VCL: Traitorous Eight and the planar process (dual Perplexity and Gemini audit; Wikipedia, Britannica, PBS American Experience, ETHW, Linda Hall Library, History Tools, IT History Society)

nodes.label: Eight Shockley Semiconductor scientists meet secretly at San Francisco's Clift Hotel to plan their departure; ten one-dollar bills are signed as the founding contract
Fairchild Semiconductor is formed with Sherman Fairchild's $1.3M backing (dates vary by source; the post states only 1957)
Jean Hoerni conceives the planar process, leaving silicon's own grown oxide in place to seal transistor junctions against contamination
Noyce conceives the monolithic integrated circuit on Hoerni's planar surface; Fairchild files the planar patent; Fairchild Camera exercises its buyout and each founder receives $250,000

nodes.name: Jean Hoerni
nodes.note: Swiss-born physicist (1924-1997), one of the eight. Solved a contamination yield problem by leaving silicon's grown oxide over the junctions, against industry practice, and in doing so produced the flat insulated surface that made printed wiring possible. The enabling was a consequence, not the goal.

nodes.name: Robert Noyce
nodes.note: The line's namesake (1927-1990). Led the eight out of Shockley's lab; in 1959 realized the wafer need not be cut apart, components could be connected by metal lines printed over Hoerni's glass through etched holes. Co-inventor of the IC with Kilby; later co-founded Intel.

nodes.name: Gordon Moore
nodes.note: One of the eight; later co-founder of Intel and author of Moore's Law. One of the two leaders of the walkout alongside Noyce.

nodes.name: Sherman Fairchild
nodes.note: Put up $1.3 million to start Fairchild Semiconductor, retaining the buyout option exercised in 1959.

nodes.text: Shockley started Shockley Semiconductor Laboratory in 1956 in Mountain View and recruited young PhD graduates to develop semiconductor devices.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [1] (ETHW; Wikipedia)

nodes.text: His management was authoritarian and unpopular, accentuated by his research focus not proving fruitful; by early 1957 the engineers tried to have him removed from management, were refused, and eight resigned.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [2][3] (Wikipedia; Britannica)

nodes.text: The eight: Julius Blank, Victor Grinich, Jean Hoerni, Eugene Kleiner, Jay Last, Gordon Moore, Robert Noyce, Sheldon Roberts; Shockley described their leaving as a "betrayal" and they became known as the traitorous eight.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [4][5] (Wikipedia; PBS; ETHW)

nodes.text: In June 1957 they met secretly at San Francisco's Clift Hotel; they signed ten one-dollar bills, one for each of the eight and two for the bankers, as symbolic contracts.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [6][7] (PBS; Linda Hall Library; Gemini confirmed Arthur Rock produced the bills and all ten signatories signed all ten)

nodes.text: Each engineer contributed $500 of his own money; when the stakes were later sold back to Fairchild, each received $250,000.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [8] (Britannica; Gemini: $500 was roughly a month's salary; buyout exercised 1959)

nodes.text: Sherman Fairchild put up $1.3 million to start Fairchild Semiconductor, retaining a buyout option.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [9] (PBS)

nodes.text: In 1958 Hoerni engineered a process leaving a layer of silicon oxide on top of transistors, sealing junctions against dirt, dust, and contaminants; his motivation was the contamination that plagued production, a yield problem.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [11][12] (Britannica; conception 1958, patent filed 1959)

nodes.text: Industry practice was to etch the oxide away to reach the silicon; Hoerni left it on, and reliability jumped. The process also left the wafer under a flat, electrically insulating sheet, which was not the goal.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [12][13] (Britannica; History Tools; Gemini confirmed the mesa-process contrast)

nodes.text: Standard practice was to build components together on one wafer, cut them apart, and wire the pieces back together by hand; circuits had grown more complex than could be reliably assembled.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [14] (Britannica)

nodes.text: Noyce realized cutting was unnecessary: components could be created in the same wafer and connected by depositing lines of conductive metal across the oxide, through small holes etched in the protective coating.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [15][16] (Britannica; Linda Hall Library)

nodes.text: Fairchild filed a patent application for the planar process in 1959.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [17] (Britannica)

nodes.text: Jack Kilby at Texas Instruments reached a similar IC concept about six months earlier; after roughly a decade of litigation ending in a split decision and cross-licensing, both are recognized as co-inventors; Noyce's monolithic silicon version, built on Hoerni's glass, was the manufacturable one.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [18][19] (Britannica; IT History Society; Gemini: Kilby Sept 1958, germanium with flying wires)

nodes.name: Transistor junction contamination (the yield problem Hoerni was solving) and the hand-wiring limit on circuit complexity
The monolithic integrated circuit, printed wiring on a sealed wafer, the foundation of all chip manufacture since

nodes.label: B-2 enters USAF service

nodes.name: Bruce J. Hinds
nodes.note: Northrop chief test pilot; commanded the B-2's first flight.

nodes.name: Richard S. Couch
nodes.note: USAF colonel, B-2 Combined Test Force commander; co-pilot on the first flight.

nodes.name: Glen Edwards
nodes.note: Killed flight-testing the YB-49 in 1948; Edwards AFB, where the B-2 first landed, carries his name.

nodes.text: A conventional aircraft controls yaw with a rudder on a vertical tail; the B-2 has no vertical fin, so split rudders and elevons control yaw, with pitch and roll handled by the elevons.
nodes.sourceNote: The Aviationist; USAF fact sheet

nodes.text: Flying wings without rear stabilizers tend to wander in yaw; this instability defeated Northrop's 1940s flying wings.
nodes.sourceNote: HowStuffWorks; Part 1 VCL. Adjudicated: phrased at program level; the 1948 crash's specific cause was never definitively established, so instability is not stated as the cause of the crash itself.

nodes.text: The control suite is three sets of elevons per side for pitch and roll, a centerline gust load alleviation surface (GLAS) for pitch and turbulence loads, and upper and lower split drag rudders at the wingtips for yaw.
nodes.sourceNote: DTIC aeroservoelastic paper (primary); Target Lock; Gemini confirmed layout (one outer plus two inner elevons per side)

nodes.text: The drag rudders are a four-part split-flap system, each assembly with an upper and lower appendage; used independently they turn the aircraft, used together they act as speed brakes.
nodes.sourceNote: Target Lock; The Aviationist

nodes.text: To turn, the flight computer opens the split rudder on one wingtip only; drag pulls that wing back and the nose yaws toward the open side. Opening upper and lower surfaces together cancels the lift change, leaving nearly pure drag.
nodes.sourceNote: wionews; The National Interest (asymmetric drag, directional authority without fins); mechanism-level lift-cancellation kept without figures

nodes.text: The B-2 is aerodynamically unstable; a human pilot could not keep it level manually. A quadruple-redundant fly-by-wire system makes thousands of corrections per second, so precisely the pilots usually feel nothing.
nodes.sourceNote: wionews; HowStuffWorks; Part 1 VCL

nodes.text: Air Force finite-element analysis projects the airframe sound to about 40,000 flight hours; the rudder attachment points at the wingtips are the highest-stress areas, projected to fail first.
nodes.sourceNote: The Aviationist (banked; not in the published caption)

nodes.text: On July 17, 1989, AV-1 (82-1066) flew from Air Force Plant 42, Palmdale, to Edwards AFB, crewed by Hinds and Couch, gear down for the entire flight as a precaution, with F-16 chase.
nodes.sourceNote: This Day in Aviation; 131st BW (USAF); White Eagle Aerospace; Edwards AFB anniversary coverage

nodes.text: Flight duration is stated only as about two hours.
nodes.sourceNote: 1h52m (This Day in Aviation) vs 2h12m (White Eagle) vs 2h20m (131st BW). The caption deliberately prints no precise figure.

nodes.text: Edwards AFB is named for Capt. Glen Edwards, killed flight-testing the YB-49 in 1948; the B-2's first flight ended with a landing there, forty-one years later.
nodes.sourceNote: Part 1 VCL (Rule 1 reuse); first-flight sources

nodes.text: One B-2 has been lost in the type's history: Spirit of Kansas, February 2008, Guam; both pilots ejected safely.
nodes.sourceNote: White Eagle Aerospace; Wikipedia. Gemini pre-verified the Part 3 mechanism (condensation in port transducer units feeding incorrect airspeed to the air-data computer); full VCL reserved for Part 3.

nodes.name: Walter Horten
nodes.note: Co-designer of the Horten flying wings.

nodes.name: Erwin Ziller
nodes.note: Luftwaffe test pilot killed in the Ho 229 V2 crash of 18 February 1945 after engine failure.

nodes.title: EC VCL: Brooklyn Bridge wire fraud (V5.1 SOP, dual Perplexity and Gemini audit; StructureMag Griggs series, McCullough The Great Bridge, Daily Beast, Sheffielder, LSU law review, TRB). Independently re-verified 2026-07-27.

nodes.label: The Board, ready to award the wire contract to Roebling's firm for Bessemer steel, yields to public pressure and awards it to J. Lloyd Haigh for crucible steel; trustee Abram Hewitt holds the mortgage on Haigh's mill
Engineers prove Haigh's overnight wire-swap fraud; of eighty rings tested, five meet standard; an estimated 221 tons of condemned wire is already spun into the cables
Roebling privately informs trustee Henry Murphy; the Board suppresses the fraud, declines to prosecute, and orders Roebling to continue buying from Haigh

nodes.name: Washington Roebling
nodes.note: Chief engineer, directing by field glasses from Brooklyn Heights due to caisson disease. Distrusted Haigh from the start, ordered every ring tested instead of sampling, predicted the bribery attempts, caught the fraud, proposed switching suppliers, was overruled, and engineered around the crime. NOT John Augustus Roebling (died 1869), whom several sources misattribute.

nodes.name: J. Lloyd Haigh
nodes.note: Wire contractor. Swapped certified wire for rejected wire overnight, recycling good wire through inspection repeatedly; estimated $300,000 in illegitimate profits, including about $60,000 from selling Bessemer steel at crucible prices. Never prosecuted for the bridge fraud; his business failed within about two years and he later served prison time for separate check crimes.

nodes.name: Abram Hewitt
nodes.note: Bridge trustee, later mayor of New York; held the mortgage on Haigh's mill and pushed the contract award in his own financial interest.

nodes.name: Henry Murphy
nodes.note: Trustee who received Roebling's private report on July 22, 1878; the Board's suppression followed. In September 1878 he quietly moved the wrapping-wire contract to Roebling's Sons, no explanation published.

nodes.text: In December 1876 the wire contract went to J. Lloyd Haigh for crucible steel rather than to the Roebling family firm; trustee Abram Hewitt's conflict-of-interest resolution had barred the Roebling firm, which Washington Roebling co-owned, from bidding.
nodes.sourceNote: StructureMag; McCullough. Independently re-verified 2026-07-27: the published 'after public pressure' framing is not the documented cause (Hewitt's Sept 1876 conflict-of-interest resolution barring the Roebling firm, plus his mortgage on Haigh's mill per c-bb-02); the Bessemer-vs-crucible bid attribution is disputed between StructureMag and McCullough, so which steel the Roebling firm bid is not asserted.

nodes.text: Trustee Abram Hewitt owned the mortgage on Haigh's mill and pushed the award in his own financial interest.
nodes.sourceNote: Daily Beast; traces to McCullough

nodes.text: Roebling ordered every ring of wire tested at Haigh's factory before delivery, rather than sampling, and warned his inspectors to expect bribes; Haigh unsuccessfully attempted to bribe the inspectors.
nodes.sourceNote: StructureMag; Daily Beast

nodes.text: Haigh replaced accepted wire with rejected wire overnight, delivering the rejected wire under genuine certificates while certified wire cycled back through inspection repeatedly.
nodes.sourceNote: StructureMag; McCullough

nodes.text: Suspicion hardened in mid-June 1878; proof came July 5, 1878. Of eighty rings then tested, five met the standard.
nodes.sourceNote: McCullough; Sheffielder

nodes.text: Haigh's illegitimate profits were estimated at $300,000.
nodes.sourceNote: McCullough

nodes.text: Roebling estimated as much as 221 tons of rejected wire had been spun into the cables (an estimate, qualified as such in the caption; the hook compresses per house pattern).
nodes.sourceNote: StructureMag; McCullough; LSU law review

nodes.text: A suspension cable is built in the air one wire at a time, thousands of parallel wires spun over sixteen months (June 11, 1877 to October 5, 1878) and compacted into one bundle; the bad wire was interleaved at random depths and could not be removed without unspinning months of work in reverse.
nodes.sourceNote: StructureMag (spinning dates); TRB (irremovability); standard parallel-wire cable construction

nodes.text: The cables were designed with a safety factor of six; the fraud left an estimated factor of five (Roebling's own figure; one secondary source says four, logged and rejected).
nodes.sourceNote: StructureMag; Daily Beast. Conflict logged: The Wave says four

nodes.text: Because a cable's strength is the sum of its parallel wires, weakness cannot be subtracted but strength can be added around it; Roebling ordered 150 extra wires spun into each cable, supplied by Haigh free of charge.
nodes.sourceNote: StructureMag; McCullough; Daily Beast (mechanism level)

nodes.text: The Board chose not to make the fraud public, declined to switch suppliers, and ordered Roebling to continue with Haigh, suppressing the information after being informed on July 22, 1878.
nodes.sourceNote: StructureMag; Daily Beast; McCullough. Adjudicated: the trustees knew is documented (Roebling's report), not inference; softening rejected.

nodes.text: In September 1878 the wrapping-wire contract was quietly moved from Haigh to John A. Roebling's Sons at Murphy's direction, with no explanation published; the press and Hewitt stayed silent.
nodes.sourceNote: McCullough

nodes.text: A good share of what Haigh delivered was not crucible steel but Bessemer, the cheap steel the trustees had rejected, sold at the crucible price; Roebling estimated about $60,000 from this deception alone.
nodes.sourceNote: McCullough (a good percentage; caption wording aligned to source per adjudication)

nodes.text: The last wire went over on October 5, 1878, at 4:45 PM, eight months sooner than Roebling expected; the bridge opened May 24, 1883, and the condemned wire remains in the cables today.
nodes.sourceNote: McCullough; StructureMag; Sheffielder; multiple

nodes.name: Joseph Bazalgette
nodes.note: Chief engineer of the Metropolitan Board of Works (1819-1891). Hired to defeat a smell under a wrong theory of disease; his sewers stopped cholera as an undesigned consequence of moving sewage out of the tidal river Londoners drank from. Personally reviewed every connection; thousands of surviving plans carry his handwritten notes.

nodes.name: John Snow
nodes.note: Physician (1813-1858). Correctly identified cholera as waterborne via the 1854 Broad Street pump, was disbelieved, and died in June 1858 during the Great Stink itself, unvindicated; the waterborne theory of cholera gained acceptance from about 1866, though germ theory proper matured later. The man who understood the disease could not stop it; the engineer who did not understand it did.

nodes.text: In 1854 John Snow traced a cholera outbreak to the Broad Street pump in Soho and argued cholera spread through contaminated water, not bad air; he was largely disbelieved.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL (Britannica; Wikipedia John Snow; standard record)

nodes.text: Snow died in June 1858, during the Great Stink, his theory still rejected; it took roughly another eight years (to about 1866) for acceptance.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [14] (Interessia; standard record; Snow died 16 June 1858)

nodes.text: In the hot summer of 1858 the Thames was an open sewer; waste from over two million Londoners poured in and the tide carried it through the city, piled up to six feet high on the banks. Parliament soaked its curtains in chloride of lime and debated leaving London. It was called the Great Stink.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [1][2] (MIT Press/Halliday; The Engineer; slideshare record)

nodes.text: Bazalgette, chief engineer of the Metropolitan Board of Works, was tasked with removing the smell; the prevailing miasma theory held that foul air caused disease.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [13] (ICE; standard record)

nodes.text: He built 82 miles of intercepting sewers running parallel to the river, fed by more than 1,100 miles of street sewers, sloping east on gravity to carry waste far downstream; more than 300 million bricks, Portland cement used at unprecedented scale.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [5][6][7] (ICE; The Engineer; restoremag). Bricks kept as more than 300 million (318M/320M conflict logged)

nodes.text: Bazalgette used the densest population and most generous output to compute the pipe diameter needed, then doubled it, recorded by the Institution of Civil Engineers as: "We're only going to do this once and there's always the unforeseen."
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [10] (Institution of Civil Engineers, verbatim quote, 14 words)

nodes.text: The doubling multiplies gravity-flow capacity roughly sixfold, because cross-sectional area grows with the square of the diameter (x4) and Manning velocity with d^(2/3) (x about 1.6), giving flow proportional to d^(8/3) (about 6.3x). A system sized for four million serves nine million today.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [12] (standard hydraulics; Gemini independently re-derived 4 x 1.58 = about 6.3; kept over Perplexity's too-specific objection per adjudication doctrine, take the derivable number over the softening)

nodes.text: London drank from the same tidal Thames the sewage washed through; by carrying waste downstream, Bazalgette removed it from the drinking supply and stopped cholera, a waterborne disease he did not know he was fighting.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [4][13] (standard record; the myth-vs-reality core). Adjudicated: framed as reducing cholera, not ended a single epidemic (precision fix taken)

nodes.text: The combined system now spills into the Thames in heavy rain, so London built the Thames Tideway Tunnel (25 km, opened 2025) to cut overflows by about 95%; the delivery company is Bazalgette Tunnel Ltd and the new riverside is Bazalgette Embankment.
nodes.sourceNote: VCL [15][17] (Wikipedia; ScienceDirect; BBC). Cost deliberately omitted (source conflict)
